issues.legal_issue: A contractual deadline is not essential where the agreement requires the seller to clear a mortgage and obtain the title documents before the buyer must pay the balance.
material_facts: The agreement required payment of the balance within three months but also required the seller to obtain title documents held by a mortgagee after the mortgage was cleared.
The agreement required the buyer to settle the loan and provided for the seller to execute the sale deed when the balance was paid.
The courts below granted specific performance, and the High Court reversed their judgments on the ground that the three-month period made time essential.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to treat the three-month period as essential because the seller's obligation to clear the mortgage and obtain the title documents had to be performed first.
issues.legal_principle: The agreement must be read as a whole: where promises are reciprocal and the seller must first clear an encumbrance and obtain title documents, the buyer's obligation to pay the balance follows that performance. The Court relied on the terms of the agreement, particularly clauses 3, 5 and 8; it cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.seller_must_clear_mortgage_first: The agreement requires the seller to clear a mortgage and obtain title documents before the transaction can be completed.
predicates.buyer_balance_due_after_title_documents: The agreement makes payment of the buyer's balance due after the seller obtains the title documents.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance case involves an agreement requiring the seller to clear a mortgage and obtain title documents before the buyer pays the balance, the contractual deadline is not essential.

issues.legal_issue: A registered notice returned undelivered is deemed served when it was sent to the recipient's proper address and the recipient does not rebut that basis for service.
material_facts: The buyer sent two registered letters to the seller's address, but they were returned with remarks that the seller had not received them for the preceding week.
The seller later received a legal notice at that same address.
The seller provided no evidence that the address was incorrect.
issues.conclusion: The returned registered letters were deemed served on the seller.
issues.legal_principle: A registered letter sent to the recipient's proper address is deemed served when it is returned with the stated remarks, unless the recipient proves otherwise. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this rule.

predicates.registered_notice_case: The proceeding concerns whether a registered notice was served on its intended recipient.
predicates.registered_letter_returned: The sender dispatched a registered letter to the recipient, and it was returned without delivery.
predicates.same_address_later_used_for_received_not: The recipient later received another notice at the same address.
predicates.recipient_did_not_rebut_address: The recipient provided no evidence that the address used for the returned letter was not the proper address.

issues.definition: A registered notice is deemed served when it was returned, a later notice reached the recipient at the same address, and the recipient did not show that the address was improper.

issues.legal_issue: Delay alone cannot defeat a timely claim for specific performance, and a short delay in filing does not negate readiness and willingness when the buyer had the funds and demonstrated readiness to complete the transaction.
material_facts: The buyer stated that he had the necessary funds and sent notices asking the seller to clear the mortgage, obtain the title documents and complete the sale.
The seller did not provide the mortgagee's address or take steps to clear the mortgage.
The buyer filed suit after a delay, but within the applicable limitation period, and deposited the balance consideration in court when filing the suit.

The trial court and first appellate court found readiness and willingness in the buyer's favour; the High Court reversed those findings in part based on delay and its view that readiness and willingness had not been shown.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to rely on the delay in filing suit to reject readiness and willingness or deny specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: In India, where a specific-performance suit is filed within the statutory limitation period, delay alone is not a ground to refuse relief. The Court relied on Mademsetty Satyanarayana v. G. Yelloji Rao, AIR 1965 SC 1405, paragraph 7, and on the evidence of the buyer's funds and communications demonstrating readiness to perform.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.suit_within_limitation: The buyer filed the specific-performance suit within the applicable limitation period.
predicates.buyer_had_funds_and_communicated_readine: The buyer had the funds required to complete the purchase and communicated readiness to proceed.
predicates.seller_failed_to_complete_prior_obligati: The seller did not perform an obligation that had to be completed before the buyer could pay the balance and complete the purchase.
predicates.suit_filed_after_delay: The buyer filed the suit after a delay following the agreement.

issues.definition: If a buyer with funds communicates readiness, the seller fails to complete a prior obligation, and the buyer files a specific-performance suit within the limitation period despite delay, the delay alone does not defeat the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A later estimate of property value does not justify refusing specific performance when the contract-date value was lower and the agreed price resulted from negotiation.
material_facts: The parties agreed to sell the property for Rs.3,65,000 when its value at the time of the agreement was approximately Rs.6 lakhs.
The High Court referred to a value of Rs.10 lakhs, although the evidence placed that value at the time of the plaintiff's cross-examination rather than at the agreement date.
The defendant did not prove that the property was worth Rs.10 lakhs when the agreement was made.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's erroneous assumption that the property had been sold at a throwaway price could not support refusing specific performance.
issues.legal_principle: The value of property at a later date does not establish its value at the time of the agreement; parties may negotiate a price above or below the property's value. The Court cited no statutory provision or earlier case for this issue.

predicates.specific_performance_case: The proceeding seeks specific performance of an agreement to sell.
predicates.parties_negotiated_contract_price: The parties agreed on a sale price through negotiation.
predicates.contract_date_value_lower_than_later_val: The property's value when the agreement was made was lower than a value attributed to it at a later time.
predicates.higher_value_not_proved_for_contract_dat: The party relying on the higher value did not prove that the property had that value when the agreement was made.

issues.definition: When parties negotiated a contract price and the higher property value was established only for a later time, that later value alone does not justify refusing specific performance.
